topics: 🍷 Breaking the Cup — Rav Ashi and Rav Hamnuna Zuti temper excessive joy at wedding feasts
🙏 The Right Frame of Mind — pray only from a conclusive halakha and the joy of a mitzva, never from sorrow or laughter
👋 Parting With Torah — take leave of a friend with a matter of halakha so that he remembers you
🪟 Daniel, David, Solomon — windows, three fixed prayers, facing Jerusalem, praise before requests
🕯️ Hannah's Prayer — Rav Hamnuna and Rabbi Elazar mine I Samuel 1 for the halakhot of the Amida
👦 Samuel Rules Before Eli — 'for this youth I prayed' and the danger of ruling before one's teacher

overview.title: 📖 Overview: How to Approach Prayer
overview.subtitle: Berakhot 31a–31b
overview.hebrewSource: וְחַנָּה הִיא מְדַבֶּרֶת עַל לִבָּהּ, רַק שְׂפָתֶיהָ נָּעוֹת, וְקוֹלָהּ לֹא יִשָּׁמֵעַ
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf opens with sages breaking precious cups at weddings to check unrestrained laughter, and Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai's rule that one may not fill his mouth with mirth in this world. From there the Gemara turns to the atmosphere from which one rises to pray: not judgment or open halakhic debate, not sorrow, laziness or frivolity, but a conclusive halakha and the joy of a mitzva. A Tosefta then derives the structure of prayer from Daniel, David and Solomon, and Rav Hamnuna shows how many halakhot flow from the single verse describing Hannah's silent prayer. The amud closes with Hannah's bold words to Eli and to God, and the story of young Samuel ruling in the presence of his teacher.

slides.title: 🙏 From What State Does One Rise to Pray?
slides.subtitle: Two baraitot on the atmosphere that should precede the Amida, and how to take leave of a friend

boxes.title: Not from…
items: Judgment (דִּין) or deliberation over an unsettled halakha — they distract
Laughter, conversation, frivolity, or purposeless matters

boxes.title: Rather from…
items: A conclusive halakha (הֲלָכָה פְּסוּקָה) that leaves no room for further debate
The joy of a mitzva (שִׂמְחָה שֶׁל מִצְוָה)
The Sages acted like our mishna (gravity); Rav Ashi acted like the baraita (a conclusive halakha)

boxes.title: Taking leave of a friend
items: Not from conversation, laughter or idle talk, but from a matter of halakha
The early prophets ended with words of praise and consolation
Mari, grandson of Rav Huna: this way he will remember you
Rav Kahana escorted Rav Shimi bar Ashi to the palm grove of Babylonia and learned there that the palms date from Adam's decree (Jeremiah 2:6)

callout.label: The sages and laughter:
callout.text: Rav Ashi broke a cup of costly white glass at his son's wedding when the Sages grew too merry. Rav Hamnuna Zuti, asked to sing, sang 'Woe unto us, for we shall die,' with the chorus 'Where is Torah and where is mitzva that protect us?' Rabbi Yoḥanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai: one may not fill his mouth with laughter in this world — only 'then' (Psalms 126:2), when the nations say 'the Lord has done great things.' Reish Lakish never did so again after hearing this.

slides.title: ⚖️ What Counts as a 'Conclusive Halakha'?
slides.subtitle: Three amoraim offer a model ruling that settles the mind before prayer

steps.content: 1️⃣ The Gemara asks: what is an example of a הֲלָכָה פְּסוּקָה?
2️⃣ Abaye: the ruling of Rabbi Zeira — the daughters of Israel were stringent upon themselves, so that even for a drop of blood the size of a mustard seed a woman sits seven clean days
3️⃣ Rava: the ruling of Rav Hoshaya — a person may use artifice and bring his grain into the courtyard still in its chaff, so his animal may eat it exempt from tithes
4️⃣ If you wish: the ruling of Rav Huna citing Rabbi Zeira — one who lets blood from a consecrated animal, benefit from that blood is forbidden and one who uses it commits me'ila
5️⃣ Each is a settled, universally accepted ruling — it focuses the mind without dragging it into argument

callout.label: Rabbi Akiva's custom:
callout.text: Rabbi Yehuda taught: with the congregation Rabbi Akiva would shorten his prayer and finish, to avoid burdening the public. Alone, one would leave him in one corner and find him in another — because of his many bows and prostrations.

slides.title: 🪟 The Tosefta Learns Prayer From Daniel, David, Solomon and Hannah
slides.subtitle: A series of 'I might have thought…' resolved by the prayers of biblical figures
rows: One may pray anywhere
Daniel: 'open windows facing Jerusalem' (Daniel 6:11) — Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba
Always pray in a house with windows
One may pray all day long
Daniel: 'three times a day he knelt'
There are fixed prayers
Fixed prayer began only in exile
Daniel: 'just as he had done before'
It predates the exile
One may face any direction
Daniel: 'facing Jerusalem'
Pray toward Jerusalem
All three prayers may be said at once
David: 'evening and morning and noon' (Psalms 55:18)
Each prayer at its time
One may pray aloud
Hannah: 'her voice could not be heard' (I Samuel 1:13)
The Amida is silent
Ask one's needs first, praise after
Solomon: 'to hear the song and the prayer' (I Kings 8:28) — song = praise, prayer = request
Praise first; no requests after emet veyatziv until the Amida's request blessings

callout.label: After the Amida:
callout.text: Rav Ḥiyya bar Ashi citing Rav: although personal requests belong in 'Who listens to prayer', after finishing the Amida one may add requests without limit — even the equivalent of the Yom Kippur confession.

slides.title: 🕯️ Rav Hamnuna: 'How Many Great Halakhot From the Verses of Hannah!'
slides.subtitle: Each phrase of I Samuel 1:13–17 yields a rule of prayer or of human conduct

nodes.content: 📜 וְחַנָּה הִיא מְדַבֶּרֶת עַל לִבָּהּ — 'Hannah spoke in her heart': one who prays must focus his heart
👄 'Only her lips moved': one must enunciate the words with his lips, not merely think them
🤫 'Her voice could not be heard': it is forbidden to raise one's voice in the Amida
🍷 'Eli thought her to be drunk': a drunk person is forbidden to pray — Rabbi Elazar adds: one who prays drunk is like an idolater, from bat beliya'al / benei beliya'al (Deut. 13:14)

columns.label: Rabbi Elazar on Eli
columns.content: 'How long will you be drunk?' — one who sees something unseemly in another must rebuke him. 'Go in peace… may God grant your request' — one who suspected wrongly must appease and even bless the other.

columns.label: Rabbi Elazar on Hannah
columns.content: 'I have drunk neither wine nor liquor' — one falsely suspected must inform the suspecter of his innocence. 'No, my master' (Ulla): you are no master in this matter, and the Divine Spirit does not rest on you.

callout.label: Lord of Hosts:
callout.text: Rabbi Elazar: from Creation no one called God צְבָאוֹת until Hannah. She argued: of all the hosts You created, is it hard to give me one son? Like a poor man who pushes into the king's feast: from this whole banquet, is one slice of bread too much?

slides.title: 👦 Samuel Rules Before His Teacher — and Hannah Intervenes
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Elazar reads 'for this youth I prayed' (I Samuel 1:27) as a plea for the boy's life

lines.speaker: Eli
lines.text: They slaughtered the bull — call a priest to come and slaughter it.

lines.speaker: Samuel
lines.text: Why search for a priest? Slaughter of an offering by a non-priest is valid! שְׁחִיטָה בְּזָר כְּשֵׁרָה

lines.speaker: Samuel
lines.text: Does it say 'and the priest shall slaughter'? It says 'and the priests shall offer' — only from receiving the blood onward is it a priestly mitzva.

lines.speaker: Eli
lines.text: You have spoken well. But you have ruled in the presence of your teacher, and whoever rules before his teacher is liable to death.

lines.speaker: Hannah
lines.text: 'I am the woman who stood here with you' — do not punish the child born of my prayer.

lines.speaker: Eli
lines.text: Let me punish him, and I will pray for mercy that God give you a greater son than this one.

lines.speaker: Hannah
lines.text: 'For this youth I prayed' — I want no other.

callout.label: Also from Hannah:
callout.text: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: 'who stood here with you' teaches that it is forbidden to sit within four cubits of one who is praying. And Rabbi Elazar: Hannah spoke impertinently toward Heaven — 'she prayed on the Lord' — as did Elijah at Carmel: 'You have turned their hearts backward.'

summary.principle: Prayer demands the right inner state — settled, focused, joyful in mitzva and silent in speech — and the Bible's great prayers, above all Hannah's, are the source of its halakhot.

flowSteps.content: 🍷 Excess laughter is checked: cups broken at weddings; no filling the mouth with mirth in this world (R' Shimon ben Yoḥai)
❓ From what state does one rise to pray? Not judgment, open debate, sorrow, laziness or frivolity
✅ From a conclusive halakha (R' Zeira, Rav Hoshaya, Rav Huna) and the joy of a mitzva; part from a friend with halakha

columns.content: 🪟 Daniel, David, Solomon: windows, three fixed times, face Jerusalem, praise before requests
🕯️ Hannah: focus the heart, move the lips, no raised voice, no praying drunk

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: Rebuke what is unseemly, clear yourself when wrongly suspected, appease and bless one you wronged — and never rule before your teacher

quiz.q: Why did Rav Ashi break a cup of valuable white glass at his son's wedding feast?
o: To fulfill the custom of breaking a glass under the wedding canopy
Because he saw the Sages were excessively joyous and wanted to sober them
As a sign of mourning for the Temple during the meal
Because the cup had become ritually impure
quiz.e: The Gemara relates that Rav Ashi saw the Sages 'excessively joyous' and broke the cup before them, and they became sad — a way of restraining unbounded laughter in this world.

quiz.q: According to the baraita, from what atmosphere should one begin to pray?
o: Directly from a court case, so justice is fresh in mind
From deliberation over an unresolved halakhic question
From a conclusive halakha (halakha pesuka) and the joy of a mitzva
From lighthearted conversation that relaxes the mind
quiz.e: One may not pray directly from judgment or from an unsettled halakhic debate, nor from sorrow, laziness, laughter or idle matters, but from a conclusive halakha that leaves no room for further deliberation and from the joy of a mitzva.

quiz.q: What does the Tosefta derive from Solomon's phrase 'to hear the song and the prayer' (I Kings 8:28)?
o: That prayer must be sung aloud in the Temple
That one should first praise God and only afterward request his needs
That personal requests may never be added to prayer
That the Amida must be recited three times a day
quiz.e: 'Song' is praise and 'prayer' is request; hence one does not insert requests after emet veyatziv, but begins with praise and only then asks for his needs. After the Amida, however, one may add even the equivalent of the Yom Kippur confession.

quiz.q: How does Rabbi Akiva refute Rabbi Yishmael's reading that a sota found innocent, if barren, will be granted children?
o: Barren women would deliberately seclude themselves in order to be granted children
The verse speaks only of the priest, not the woman
Hannah was never actually barren
The sota waters were never administered in practice
quiz.e: Rabbi Akiva argues that if innocence alone brought children, every barren woman would go seclude herself; rather the verse promises easier childbirth — tall instead of short, fair instead of dark, two instead of one. On his view Hannah's double 'im ra'o tireh' is simply ordinary human language.

quiz.q: What did Shmuel say Hannah meant by praying for 'an offspring of men' (zera anashim)?
o: A son who would be inconspicuous among men
A son equal to Moses and Aaron
A son who would anoint two men as kings — Saul and David
A son who would be neither too tall nor too short
quiz.e: Rav said 'a man among men'; Shmuel said an offspring who would anoint two men, Saul and David; Rabbi Yoḥanan said one weighed against Moses and Aaron (Psalms 99:6); the Rabbis said one inconspicuous among men, which Rav Dimi spelled out as neither too tall nor short, smart nor foolish.
